## Highlights

- •

The Internet has had equalizing and then polarizing effects on national urban hierarchies.
- •

In countries with a high level of economic development and trade openness, the Internet helps polarize urban hierarchies.
- •

At first, Internet reduced transportation costs and partially replaced transportation needs, equalizing urban hierarchies.
- •

Later, Internet increased the production efficiency and industrial transformation of large cities, polarizing urban hierarchies.

## Abstract

As Internet adoption and diffusion continues worldwide, little is known about its effects on the restructuring of national urban hierarchies globally. We create a city population panel data with uniform definitions within each of the 133 countries from 2000 to 2018 to study the effect of the Internet on national urban hierarchies and to examine the channels through which the effects take place. Results show that the Internet led to the equalization of urban hierarchies in the early stage and then the polarization. Initially, the Internet helped reduce communication costs, partially replaced transportation, and weakened the agglomeration of enterprises and individuals in large cities, thereby flattening national urban hierarchies. Later, the Internet mainly enhanced the production efficiency and accelerated the shift from manufacturing to services in large cities, thus increasing the large cities' attractiveness and ultimately polarizing the urban hierarchy. Our finding demonstrates that national urban hierarchies are not static and their evolution reflects not only the trade-off between economies of scale and congestion, but increasingly by the Internet—a powerful communication tool. If the trend persists, larger cities will grow at a faster pace than smaller cities and potentially increase regional inequality in countries that have extensively adopted the Internet.

## Introduction

The relative sizes of cities reflect the trade-off between economies of scale and congestion (Batty, 2008). Cities grow in size to facilitate the division of labor and generate scale economics. City sizes within a country tend to follow a power-law pattern on a cumulative curve, mirroring a Pareto distribution (Gabaix, 1999, Gabaix, 1999). This pattern is observed in various countries that went through different development stages (e.g., Eaton & Eckstein, 1997; Glaeser et al., 1995; Soo, 2005); it has been a major concern in the literature of regional science and urban geography and described by Paul Krugman as “striking empirical regularity with no good theory to account for it” (Krugman, 1996).

The spatial organization of individuals and economic activities has evolved over time. The evolution is particularly evident in the restructuring of the urban hierarchy. While urban hierarchy studies have explored functional linkages between cities and, more recently, examined the structures in world city networks (e.g., Smith & Timberlake, 2001; Taaffe, 1962), much effort has been devoted to the study of the rank-size distribution of cities and its determinants (e.g., Angel, 2012; Henderson, 1974; Zipf, 1941). Theoretically, cities grow and decline due to local innovations, exogenous idiosyncratic shocks on their amenities, and the subsequent migration of young workers (Duranton, 2002; Eeckhout, 2004; Gabaix, 1999, Gabaix, 1999). However, there is limited empirical evidence of support. Taylor (1997) made an urgent call for “global-scale analyses” of urban hierarchies “within a broader space-time context” rather than the static conception of urban hierarchy in the literature. Although many studies have examined the pattern of city size distribution since then, few have looked beyond selected countries or through a longitudinal framework.

The Internet has been increasingly adopted as a means of communication and production, becoming an important factor in urban growth (or decline) and providing a unique opportunity to study its associated effects on urban hierarchies. Most empirical studies have focused on its effect on the agglomerations or dispersions of industries and production factors within cities and the resulting changes in intracity spatial structures (e.g., Dadashpoor & Yousefi, 2018). Empirical evidence suggests that Internet access and diffusion is associated with growing regional disparity and consumption inequality, by facilitating migration to more productive cities and thus increasing the spatial divergence between cities (Lin et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2020; Wu et al., 2019). The Internet has accelerated the movements of individuals and economic activities (Zhen et al., 2015). However, few existing studies have examined the effect of the Internet on intercity urban spatial structure—urban hierarchies; the results are inconsistent (e.g., Ioannides et al., 2008; Paschke, 2019; Tranos & Ioannides, 2020; Tranos & Ioannides, 2021; Wang et al., 2021).

The International Telecommunication Union (ITU) notes in the State of Broadband 2018 Report that access to information and communication technologies is becoming increasingly unequal within and between countries, leading to a widening gap in national economic growth and competitiveness. To mitigate this growing concern, ITU advocates that every country should have an Internet or broadband strategy in place by 2025. A growing number of countries have recognized the importance of the Internet in their economic development and urban growth. Evidently, 159 countries had developed some Internet or broadband strategies by 2018; many have prioritized the building of nationwide high-speed, accessible Internet to enhance national competitiveness 1 (Guo & Luo, 2016; ITU & UNESCO, 2018). This have sparked heated discussions about the effect of the Internet on urban hierarchies. Recent developments, such as telecommunications in the SOHO model (Ohta, 2001), residential decentralizations (Wang et al., 2021), and the relocation of firms from urban centers to peripheries or smaller cities (Henderson & Ono, 2008), have convinced many that the Internet will lead to the “death of distance” (Cairncross, 2001) and ultimately make us closer to “the world is flat” (Friedman, 2005). As such, the urban hierarchy should have been flattening. In contrast, other scholars have argued that the Internet may further the spatial polarization of individuals and economic activities. Evidently, there has been the agglomeration of innovative talents in Silicon Valley and the growing prominence of financial services centers such as New York City (Audirac, 2002).

Little attention has been given to the channels through which the Internet has affected urban hierarchies over time. Although there are theoretical studies on possible channels (e.g., Ioannides et al., 2008; Tranos & Ioannides, 2021; Wang et al., 2021), there is little empirical validation. Given that urbanization is continuing worldwide and that a growing number of countries have elevated their Internet strategies to the national level, it is critical to examine how the Internet has affected urban hierarchies so as to improve spatial planing for the Internet era.

To fill these research gaps, this paper uses the Pareto index to measure the degree of equalization and polarization of the urban hierarchy of individual country, using a panel data of city population with uniform definitions within each of the 133 countries worldwide from 2000 to 2018. 2 We rely on a panel two-way fixed effects model and an IV approach, examining the causal links between the Internet and urban hierarchies across countries. Overall, we find specific, nonlinear effects of the Internet on urban hierarchies: equalization in the beginning of the study period, followed by polarization. However, this effect depends on the levels of economic development and trade openness at the national level. In addition, we find that the Internet has reduced communication costs and partially replaced transportation in the early stage, equalizing the urban hierarchy. Meanwhile, it has had a polarizing effect later by increasing the productivity and accelerating the industrial transformation of large cities to service industries.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: The following section covers research progress related to the effect of the Internet on urban hierarchies and the means through which the effect takes place. Section 3 describes the methodology and data. Section 4 presents the results of the empirical analyses and Section 5 summarizes our findings and provides our conclusions.

### Measurement of urban hierarchies

Data incompatibility has made it difficult, if not impossible, to compare city populations across the world. Existing global city population databases have inconsistent definitions of city boundary between countries. Some are based on administrative definitions, e.g., the prefecture-level city in China, while others use functional definitions such as urban agglomeration or economic regions in the U.S. (Berry & Okulicz-Kozaryn, 2012; Sun et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
